paper_metadata.title: Knowledge Vault: A Web-Scale Approach to Probabilistic Knowledge Fusion
paper_metadata.abstract: The paper introduces Knowledge Vault, a Web-scale probabilistic knowledge base that combines extractions from Web content—including text, tabular data, page structure, and human annotations—with prior knowledge from existing repositories. Supervised machine-learning fusion computes calibrated probabilities that candidate facts are correct, and the paper studies the utility of the sources and extraction methods.

problem_addressed: Constructing a much larger knowledge base from the Web while controlling the noise of automatic extraction. The objective is to populate a fixed-schema, language-independent repository of disambiguated RDF triples and attach a calibrated probability of correctness to every candidate fact by combining Web extraction evidence with graph-derived Freebase priors.

methodology.description: Execution pipeline: (1) collect Web free text, HTML DOM trees, HTML tables, and schema.org-annotated pages; (2) for text, run named-entity recognition, POS tagging, dependency parsing, within-document coreference, and entity linking, then train per-predicate distant-supervision logistic-regression extractors from surface/dependency patterns; (3) for DOM pages, learn classifiers from lexicalized DOM paths between linked entities; (4) for tables, link entities and match each unambiguous column to a Freebase predicate; (5) map a subset of schema.org annotations manually to Freebase predicates; (6) merge/de-duplicate source evidence at domain level and fuse the four extractor outputs with per-predicate boosted decision stumps; (7) learn graph priors from Freebase with PRA random-walk path features and a 60-dimensional embedding/MLP link-prediction model, then fuse the priors; (8) fuse extraction and prior scores and calibrate output probabilities with Platt scaling. Labels for supervised training and most testing use the local closed-world assumption (LCWA).

ontology_or_schema_use.value: The system uses a fixed ontology: entity types and predicates are fixed, and outputs use Freebase entity identifiers and predicates. Freebase supplies both schema and prior facts. HTML-table columns are matched to Freebase predicates; schema.org annotations are manually mapped to 14 mostly person-related Freebase predicates. This constrains extraction but leaves Web entities and relations absent from Freebase unsupported in the current system.

input_output.input_type: Web-scale unstructured and semi-structured Web content: free text documents, HTML DOM trees, HTML tables, and human-authored schema.org annotations; existing Freebase triples are also input as graph priors and distant-supervision seeds.
input_output.input_granularity: Document/page-level text and DOM trees; table-column-level Web tables; page annotations; linked entity-pair/sentence instances for text extraction; and candidate subject–predicate–object triples for fusion and graph-prior scoring.
input_output.output_representation: A probabilistic, weighted labeled knowledge graph of disambiguated RDF subject–predicate–object triples, using fixed Freebase entity identifiers and predicates. Each triple has a calibrated probability/confidence of being correct.

Boosted decision stumps for extraction/prior fusion

datasets: A very large Web corpus comprising free text, HTML DOM pages (including text and deep-Web sources), HTML tables, and schema.org-annotated pages
Freebase: source of existing triples for distant-supervision seeds, LCWA labels, and graph-prior training
Approximately 1.6 billion extracted candidate triples covering 4,469 relation types and 1,100 entity types
Balanced held-out test sample: 20% split of candidate triples, capped at 10,000 instances per predicate
Human-labeled subset: 1,000 triples across 10 predicates; 305 unknown labels discarded

metrics: Number of triples above confidence thresholds 0.7 and 0.9
Calibration comparison of estimated and true probabilities
baselines: Individual extraction systems: TBL, ANO, TXT, and DOM
Individual graph-prior methods: PRA and MLP
Prior-only and extractor-only systems compared with the fused prior-plus-extractor system
LCWA labels compared with human labels for the same fused systems
evaluation.setting: Candidate triples were randomly split 80%/20% for training/testing, with the exact same triple excluded from training and each predicate capped at 10,000 test instances before pooling to balance common predicates. Labels were generated by LCWA: a Freebase-listed object is positive, an alternative object for a locally nonempty subject–predicate pair is negative, and empty pairs are dropped. Extraction-system AUCs use their distinct corresponding test sets; fused-extractor AUC uses their union. A human assessment used in-house raters on 1,000 triples from 10 predicates, retaining 695 non-unknown judgments; models remained trained on the full LCWA-labelled training data.

value: The completed KV contains 1.6B candidate triples; 271M have probability at least 0.9, cover 4,469 relation types and 1,100 entity types, and about one-third of these confident facts are not already in Freebase.

Among individual extractors, DOM has the highest AUC (0.928), followed by ANO (0.920), TXT (0.867), and TBL (0.856). Fusing extractors yields 100M facts at confidence at least 0.9 versus 94M for DOM alone, with AUC 0.927.
PRA and the 60-dimensional MLP graph prior have similar AUCs (0.884 and 0.882); fusing those priors raises AUC to 0.911.

Combining fused extractor evidence with fused graph priors raises high-confidence facts from about 100M to about 271M and achieves AUC 0.959 under LCWA labels, compared with 0.943 prior-only and 0.872 extractor-only.

On human judgments, performance is lower but the combined system remains best: AUC 0.869 versus 0.852 extractor-only and 0.843 prior-only. The authors interpret the limited degradation as indirect support for LCWA adequacy.
The calibrated fused probability has the stated interpretation that about 90% of triples assigned 0.9 are true.

value: The architecture integrates complementary evidence: four heterogeneous Web extraction modalities, Freebase graph priors, and learned per-predicate fusion rather than trusting any individual extractor.
It produces calibrated uncertainty rather than only binary facts, enabling the system to distinguish high-confidence from uncertain facts.
It operates at Web scale and achieves high coverage: 271M facts at probability at least 0.9, including roughly one-third absent from the prior Freebase graph.
The empirical design separately measures extractor, prior, and fused performance and includes a human-label check of LCWA-based evaluation.
[Review inference] The fixed Freebase schema and entity identifiers make the output directly interoperable as a structured KG and suppress lexical relation duplication typical of open IE.

value: The system treats facts as independent binary variables for scalability, so it does not model mutual exclusion or other correlations among facts.
LCWA-derived labels are imperfect because Freebase is incomplete and can contain errors; human-label AUCs are lower than LCWA AUCs.
The fixed Freebase ontology excludes Web entities and relations not already representable in Freebase; automatic creation of new entities remains work in progress.
Simple domain-level source deduplication does not adequately address copied or correlated sources.
The system does not model temporal validity of facts and supports only simple probabilistic queries, not JOIN or SELECT.

[Review inference] The paper evaluates globally pooled, predicate-balanced AUC and confidence counts, so it does not report end-to-end precision/recall by extraction source, entity type, or individual predicate; deployment behavior for rare or newly introduced schemas is therefore not established here.

value: LCWA is only an approximation: Freebase's partial actor lists can create false negatives and Freebase errors can create false positives.
For scalability, the current model treats each fact independently and does not enforce mutual exclusion for functional relations.
Naively enforcing mutual exclusion fails when values differ only in granularity, such as Honolulu versus Hawaii.
Soft numerical correlations among facts are not fully integrated.
The current compatibility handling across abstraction levels is limited to geographical knowledge.
Counting each domain once is only a simple treatment of duplicated or correlated sources.
The current system lacks temporal fact modeling; fact duration is not necessarily linked to source timestamp.
Entities absent from Freebase and relations outside its schema cannot currently be represented.
RDF triples may be inadequate for richer forms of knowledge, and a fixed ontology has a difficult long tail of concepts.
Even perfect Web machine reading cannot recover all human knowledge, especially commonsense knowledge unavailable on the Web.

value: How to learn reliable truth probabilities when the existing KB used for weak labels is incomplete or erroneous.
How to jointly model hard mutual exclusion and soft fact correlations at Web scale without conflating semantically compatible values at different granularities.
How to identify copied or correlated Web sources so repeated evidence is not overcounted.
How to represent time-varying facts when a source timestamp does not determine a fact's validity interval.
How to add new entities and relation types while avoiding uncontrolled redundant or synonymous relations.
How to represent richer conceptual/commonsense knowledge beyond a fixed RDF triple ontology and obtain knowledge not expressed on the Web.

[Review inference] These limitations jointly leave open a central quality-control problem: scalable KG population must reconcile evidence provenance, entity/schema expansion, and interdependent fact constraints rather than scoring candidate triples independently.
